supported_claims.text: Early forms of 元 are interpreted as a human figure with a mark emphasizing the head. The head is the proposed pictorial referent; a division into the modern-looking parts 儿 and 二 is not established.

The received Shuowen glosses 元 as ‘beginning’ and analyzes it as 一 plus 兀. Later interpreters disagree whether 兀 is a sound element or contributes the head sense; neither interpretation independently establishes the graph’s original formation.

The cited oracle-bone example 元卜 is interpreted as ‘first divination’; cited Western Zhou bronze uses include 元年 ‘first year’ and 元德 ‘great virtue.’ These support early uses meaning ‘first/beginning’ and ‘great,’ but the cited inscriptions do not use 元 to mean ‘head.’
The transmitted Zuo zhuan passage 狄人歸其元 uses 元 for ‘head.’ Its transcription is evidence for that textual use, not a dated manuscript witness.

The early head interpretation and inscriptional ‘first/beginning’ uses are distinct claims. A development from ‘head’ to ‘first/beginning’ is proposed, but the dossier does not document a dated sequence demonstrating that transition.
The curated image is a modern digital redraw in a Shuowen seal-script style. It illustrates that style, not an ancient artifact or the earliest head-marked form.

disagreements.text: The early graph is interpreted as a human figure with a mark at the head, while a modern-stroke account describes a person 儿 with 二 emphasizing the head. The exact identification of the early strokes as 儿 plus 二 is not established.
The received Shuowen analysis 从一从兀 is construed differently: one interpretation treats 兀 as a phonetic element, while another treats it as contributing the head sense in an associative analysis.
An alternative analysis takes the upper strokes as 上 above 人. The paleographic account challenges that reading against early forms with a point marking the head.
A proposal treats 元 and 兀 as split forms from one graph. The dossier reports this proposal but does not establish it as the graph’s origin.

limitations.text: The dossier supports a pictorial reading of the whole early graph but does not establish a distinct internal component split. No components or component sound comparisons are warranted; the Shuowen breakdown is a later analysis, not independent proof of the original construction.
The cited inscriptional uses are identified by period and context, but exact dates were not established. The transmitted Zuo zhuan and Mengzi examples are not manuscript dating evidence.

The meanings ‘head’ and ‘first/beginning’ are supported in different evidence, but the precise semantic path between them is not documented here. The dossier does not establish whether ‘great’ developed from either meaning or by another route.

The dossier gives modern Mandarin yuán and character-level historical readings, but no independently established sound component or ancient pronunciation for an underlying depicted object. It therefore cannot support a phonetic-component claim or a sound comparison for 元’s construction.
